title: The Take-Home Architecture Exercise
summary: The async design-doc or architecture-proposal exercise some senior/staff loops use instead of, or alongside, a live whiteboard round.

slides.markdown:
Some senior and staff loops replace, or supplement, the live whiteboard round with a take-home exercise: write a design doc or proposal for a given system, submitted asynchronously over a few days instead of live in 45 minutes.

It's graded on the same axes as a live round — problem understanding, trade-off reasoning, communication — just without the time pressure, and with a different failure mode: nobody's there to ask you a clarifying question, so the writing has to do that work itself. This topic covers how to structure and scope the submission.

A take-home architecture exercise typically asks for a written artifact — a design doc, a set of diagrams, or both — describing how you'd build a specified system. It is explicitly not asking for working code; submitting a partial implementation instead of a design document usually signals you misread the prompt rather than that you went above and beyond.

The deliverable is your reasoning made legible on paper: what you'd build, why, and what you considered and rejected. That's a different skill from live whiteboarding — it rewards clear written communication as much as the underlying design judgment.

slides.sectionTitle: Why it's graded on the same axes, minus the time pressure
slides.markdown:
The evaluation criteria don't change from a live round: does the candidate understand the problem, reason clearly about trade-offs, and land on a defensible design. What changes is that you have days instead of minutes, so there's no excuse for skipping a consideration you'd have had time to think through — an evaluator reading a take-home holds it to a higher bar of thoroughness precisely because the time constraint that would excuse gaps in a live round isn't present.

That's a double-edged sword: you can produce a more polished, more complete answer than any live round allows, but a shallow submission looks worse here than an equally shallow live answer would, because you had the time to do better.

slides.sectionTitle: Cross-link: using the design-doc structure as an interview artifact
slides.markdown:
The actual structure of a good design doc — problem statement, requirements, goals and non-goals, proposed design, alternatives considered — is covered in depth in [writing a design doc](writing-a-design-doc). That topic explains how to write one for real engineering work; this one is about the narrower question of using that same structure as an interview artifact.

The difference in application: in a real design doc, you're writing for teammates who'll actually build the thing and can ask you questions later. In a take-home, you're writing for an evaluator who won't — which means every section needs to anticipate and answer the follow-up questions a live round would have let you handle verbally.

slides.sectionTitle: Structuring the submission: problem, requirements, options, chosen design, trade-offs
slides.markdown:
A submission that reads well to an evaluator follows a predictable shape: **problem** — restate it in your own words, showing you understood the actual ask. **Requirements** — functional and non-functional, including the scale assumptions you're designing for. **Options considered** — at least two real alternatives, briefly. **Chosen design** — the architecture itself, with enough detail to be concrete. **Trade-offs** — what the chosen design costs, stated plainly rather than glossed over.

Skipping the options-considered section is the most common gap — candidates often jump straight to their chosen design, which reads as if only one option ever occurred to them, even when that's not true.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an architecture exercise submission outline
slides.markdown:

Treat this outline as a checklist before submitting — each section maps directly to something an evaluator is specifically looking for, and a missing section reads as a missing consideration, not just a missing paragraph.

slides.sectionTitle: Time-boxing the exercise instead of polishing it for days
slides.markdown:
Because there's no interviewer watching the clock, it's tempting to keep polishing for the entire window given, sometimes several days. This usually backfires: diminishing returns set in quickly after the core content is solid, and an evaluator can't tell the difference between a submission that took six focused hours and one that took three unfocused days — they're reading the document, not your calendar.

Set your own time box — often a stated or implied expectation exists, commonly a few focused hours — and stop once you've covered the five sections with real content. Extra days are better spent re-reading for clarity and gaps than adding more detail to sections that are already solid.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a live round's follow-ups vs a take-home's need to preempt them
slides.markdown:
| | Live round | Take-home |
|---|---|---|
| Clarifying questions | Interviewer asks, you answer in real time | No one to ask — you must state your own assumptions |
| Handling ambiguity | Resolved through back-and-forth dialogue | Must be resolved on the page, explicitly |
| Follow-up probes | Interviewer digs into a specific decision live | You must anticipate likely probes and answer them preemptively |
| Risk if unaddressed | A quick clarifying exchange fixes it | An unaddressed gap sits there, unfixable after submission |

The practical implication: for every place you'd normally rely on a live follow-up to clarify or defend a decision, the take-home needs a sentence doing that work in advance.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a diagram with no written rationale
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A clear architecture diagram speaks for itself — the evaluator can see the boxes and arrows and understand the design."

**Why it's wrong:** a diagram shows *what* you'd build but not *why* — without written rationale, the evaluator has to guess at your reasoning, and guesses tend to be graded conservatively. Two different reasoning processes can produce the same-looking diagram, and only the writing distinguishes a well-justified design from a lucky one.

**Correct model:** every diagram needs accompanying prose that states the reasoning behind its key decisions — the diagram illustrates the design, the writing justifies it, and a take-home submission needs both.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-scoping the design far beyond what the prompt calls for
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Since I have days instead of minutes, I should design for every scale and edge case I can think of, to show thoroughness."

**Why it's wrong:** the prompt usually specifies constraints — a target scale, a specific set of features — deliberately, and a submission that designs for 100x that scale or adds unrequested features reads as not respecting the stated constraints, not as extra effort. It also dilutes the sections that actually matter, since time spent gold-plating an unrequested feature is time not spent justifying the trade-offs the prompt did ask about.

**Correct model:** design precisely to the stated constraints, and if you want to show awareness of what's beyond scope, note it briefly as a "not addressed here" line rather than building it out — that shows judgment about scope, which is itself part of what's being evaluated.
